title: Given a list of transaction narration strings, count how often each word appears using `groupingBy` with `counting`, then return the words sorted by frequency descending. Explain counting as a downstream collector and how to sort a map by value.
shortTitle: Build a word frequency map and return the top entries sorted by count descending
keyPoints: `groupingBy(classifier, counting())` produces a `Map<K, Long>` of how many elements fall into each group.
`counting()` is a downstream collector that returns each group's size as a `Long`.
A map has no inherent order, so ranking by frequency is a separate step over the entry set.
`limit(n)` after sorting keeps only the top N entries.
Add `thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey())` as a tie-breaker so equal counts order deterministically.
Collect the ranked entries into a `LinkedHashMap` when you need to preserve the ranking in a map rather than a list.

s1_definition.oneliner: `groupingBy(word, counting())` gives a count per key; sort the entries by value descending to rank them.
s1_definition.profdef:
Counting and ranking are two distinct steps.

- **`groupingBy(classifier, counting())`** – builds a `Map<K, Long>` mapping each key to its occurrence count.
- **`counting()`** – a downstream collector that returns the number of elements in each group as a `Long`.
- **ranking by value** – stream the map's `entrySet`, sort with `Map.Entry.comparingByValue(Comparator.reverseOrder())`, and optionally `limit` to the top N.
- **tie-breaking** – chain `thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey())` so entries with equal counts order deterministically.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh tallies how often each word appears across all transaction notes, like counting how many times SALARY or RENT shows up. `counting` is the tally mark per word. Then he lines the words up with the most frequent on top, and when two words tie he orders them alphabetically so the list looks the same every time.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  narrations -> words -> frequency map

  ["SALARY CREDIT", "RENT", "SALARY"]
          │  flatMap split on whitespace
          ▼
  [SALARY, CREDIT, RENT, SALARY]
          │  groupingBy(w -> w, counting())
          ▼
  { SALARY=2, CREDIT=1, RENT=1 }   (unordered map)
```

```text
  rank by value descending

  entrySet().stream()
        │ sorted(comparingByValue(reverseOrder())
        │        .thenComparing(comparingByKey()))
        ▼
  ┌───────────┬───────┐
  │ SALARY    │   2   │  <- highest count first
  ├───────────┼───────┤
  │ CREDIT    │   1   │  <- tie broken by key (CREDIT before RENT)
  ├───────────┼───────┤
  │ RENT      │   1   │
  └───────────┴───────┘
        │ limit(topN)
        ▼
   top N ranked entries
```

```text
  keep ranking as a map

  sorted entries ──► collect(toMap(k, v, merge, LinkedHashMap::new))
                     │
                     ▼
           LinkedHashMap preserves the ranked order
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To build a frequency map I group by the value I want to count and use `counting` as the downstream collector, which gives me a map from each key to how many elements fell into that group as a `Long`. Splitting the narrations into words, normalizing case, and grouping by word with `counting` gives me the occurrence count for every word in one pass.

Ranking by frequency is a separate step, because a map has no inherent order by value. I stream the map's entry set and sort with `Map.Entry.comparingByValue` in reverse order so the most frequent entries come first, then `limit` to the top N. In my banking work at the National Bank of India I used exactly this to find the most common keywords in transaction narrations, which fed an auto-categorization feature.

The senior point I always add is tie-breaking and determinism. When two keys share the same count, I chain a secondary comparator on the key with `thenComparing` so the order is stable across runs, which matters when the output drives a report or a model. If I need the ranked result as a map rather than a list, I collect the sorted entries into a `LinkedHashMap` to preserve that order, since a plain `HashMap` would scramble it and a `TreeMap` would re-order by key rather than count.

Think of Rajesh tallying words across every transaction note: he counts each word, stacks the most frequent on top, and settles ties alphabetically so the list reads the same every time.

Remember one sentence: `groupingBy(word, counting())` builds the histogram, and sorting the entry set by value descending with a key tie-breaker ranks it deterministically.
